title: Absolute and conditional convergence
objectives: Tell absolute from conditional convergence, and prove the alternating series test.

screens.title: A zigzag that closes in
screens.prose: The dots are the partial sums of $\sum \tfrac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n} = 1 - \tfrac12 + \tfrac13 - \tfrac14 + \cdots$. Slide $n$ to compare neighbouring sums.
screens.question: What do the partial sums do?

options.text: They swing up and down by ever smaller amounts, closing in on one value near 0.69.
They settle at 0, because the terms cancel in pairs.
options.why: You paired terms that do not cancel: $1 - \tfrac12 = \tfrac12$, $\tfrac13 - \tfrac14 = \tfrac1{12}$. Each pair is positive.

options.text: They diverge, because $\sum \tfrac1n$ diverges.
options.why: You dropped the signs. With the signs, each step undoes part of the one before.

options.text: They keep swinging by about 0.5 for ever.
options.why: You read the first swing only. The swing from $S_n$ to $S_{n+1}$ is $\tfrac{1}{n+1}$, which shrinks.

hints.text: Look at the odd dots and the even dots separately.
The odd dots fall and the even dots rise.
The gap between neighbours is $\tfrac{1}{n+1}$, which tends to 0.

feedback.correct: Right. Two strands squeeze one value, $\ln 2 \approx 0.6931$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow the high dots and the low dots separately.

explain.text: The odd sums fall, the even sums rise, and each odd one sits above each even one. The gap between neighbours is $\tfrac{1}{n+1} \to 0$, so both strands meet. The common limit is $\ln 2 \approx 0.6931$.

screens.title: Four facts, four reasons
screens.prose: Let $a_n$ decrease to 0, and $S_n = a_1 - a_2 + a_3 - \cdots \pm a_n$. The proof rests on four facts. Give each its reason. Two cards are left over.
screens.question: Drag one reason onto each fact.

slots.label: Every odd sum is above every even sum.

hints.text: Each reason is one line of algebra or one known fact.
For the even sums, $S_{2n+2}$ adds $a_{2n+1}$ and takes away $a_{2n+2}$.
Decreasing terms make the first two differences signed; the third chains them; the fourth uses $a_n \to 0$.

feedback.correct: Right. Decreasing gives the first three facts; tending to 0 gives the fourth.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write each difference of partial sums out and read off its sign.

byKey.x1: You used $\sum a_n$ converging. It need not: for $a_n = \tfrac1n$ it diverges, yet every fact holds.
byKey.x2: You used the alternating signs alone. Without decreasing terms the even sums can fall; the trap will show it.
byKey.t1: Check the even sums: $S_{2n+2} = S_{2n} + a_{2n+1} - a_{2n+2}$.
byKey.t2: Check the odd sums: $S_{2n+1} = S_{2n-1} - a_{2n} + a_{2n+1}$.
byKey.t3: Every odd sum above every even sum needs the chain through $k = \max(m, n)$.
byKey.t4: The last fact is about the gap $S_{2n+1} - S_{2n} = a_{2n+1}$.

explain.text: Decreasing makes $a_{2n+1} - a_{2n+2}$ and $a_{2n} - a_{2n+1}$ non-negative, so the evens rise and the odds fall. With $k = \max(m, n)$, $S_{2m} \le S_{2k} \le S_{2k+1} \le S_{2n+1}$. The gap $a_{2n+1}$ tends to 0.

screens.title: The alternating series test proved
screens.prose: Let $a_n$ decrease to 0, and $S_n = a_1 - a_2 + a_3 - \cdots \pm a_n$. Use the four facts to prove that $\sum (-1)^{n+1} a_n$ converges. Two lines are flawed.
screens.question: Put the proof in order. Move the two flawed lines to Left out.

lines.text: The even sums rise and stay below $S_1$, so by monotone convergence $S_{2n} \to E$.
The odd sums fall and stay above $S_2$, so by monotone convergence $S_{2n+1} \to O$.
$O - E = \lim (S_{2n+1} - S_{2n}) = \lim a_{2n+1} = 0$, so $O = E$; call it $S$.
Every $n$ is even or odd, and both strands tend to $S$, so $S_n \to S$. $\blacksquare$
$(S_n)$ is bounded between $S_2$ and $S_1$ and monotone, so it converges.
lines.why: You called $(S_n)$ monotone. It zigzags; only each strand is monotone.

lines.text: $a_n \to 0$, so the series converges by the term test.
lines.why: You used the term test for convergence. It only ever proves divergence.

hints.text: Each strand is monotone and bounded.
The evens are below every odd sum, so below $S_1$; the odds are above $S_2$.
Order: the two strands (either first), their limits agree, then the whole sequence.

feedback.correct: Right. Two monotone strands with the same limit.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Get a limit for each strand, show they agree, then cover every $n$.

byKey.d2: The term test cannot prove convergence: think of $\sum \tfrac1n$.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the two flawed lines go to Left out.

explain.text: Each strand is monotone and bounded, so each converges by level 2. The gap $a_{2n+1} \to 0$ makes the limits equal. For $\varepsilon > 0$, take $N$ past which both strands are within $\varepsilon$ of $S$; then every $S_n$ with $n \ge 2N + 1$ is too.

screens.title: How far off is $S_{10}$?
screens.prose: $S$ lies between any two neighbouring partial sums, which differ by $a_{n+1}$. So $|S - S_n| \le a_{n+1}$. For $\sum \tfrac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n}$ the sum is $\ln 2$.
screens.question: What bound does the theorem give for $|\ln 2 - S_{10}|$?

hints.text: The bound is the first term not yet added.
$S_{10}$ stops at $\tfrac{1}{10}$; the next term is $\tfrac{1}{11}$.

feedback.correct: Right. $\tfrac1{11} \approx 0.0909$, and the true error 0.0475 is below it.

byKey.same: You used $a_{10} = \tfrac1{10}$, the last term added. The bound is the next one, $a_{11}$.
byKey.half: You halved the bound. The theorem gives $a_{11}$; the true error happens to be near half of it.

explain.text: $S_{10} \approx 0.645635$ and $S_{11} \approx 0.736544$ differ by $\tfrac1{11}$, and $\ln 2$ lies between them. So the error is at most $\tfrac1{11} \approx 0.0909$; in fact it is 0.047512. The bound is safe, not sharp.

screens.title: Absolute or conditional
screens.prose: A series **converges absolutely** if $\sum |a_n|$ converges. It **converges conditionally** if $\sum a_n$ converges but $\sum |a_n|$ diverges. $$\sum \tfrac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n} \text{ converges, } \sum \tfrac1n \text{ diverges: conditional.}$$
screens.question: How does $\sum \tfrac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n^2}$ converge?

options.text: Absolutely: $\sum \tfrac{1}{n^2}$ converges.
Conditionally, because the signs alternate.
options.why: You judged by the signs. The test is whether $\sum |a_n|$ converges, and $\sum \tfrac1{n^2}$ does.

options.text: Conditionally, because we proved it with the alternating series test.
options.why: You judged by the proof used. The kind of convergence depends on the series, not on the test that found it.

options.text: It diverges.
options.why: You lost the squares. $\tfrac1{n^2}$ shrinks fast; even without signs the series converges.

hints.text: Take absolute values of the terms.
$\left|\tfrac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n^2}\right| = \tfrac1{n^2}$.
$\sum \tfrac1{n^2}$ converges, so the convergence is absolute.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Decide whether $\sum |a_n|$ converges.

explain.text: $\sum \left|\tfrac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n^2}\right| = \sum \tfrac1{n^2}$ converges, so the convergence is absolute. Its sum is $\tfrac{\pi^2}{12} \approx 0.822467$, half of $\tfrac{\pi^2}{6}$. The alternating harmonic series has no such backing: its convergence is conditional.

screens.title: A block and its sizes
screens.prose: Next we prove that absolute convergence implies convergence. The proof compares a block $\sum_{k=m}^{n} a_k$ of the series with the same block of $\sum |a_k|$.
screens.question: Why is $\left|\sum_{k=m}^{n} a_k\right| \le \sum_{k=m}^{n} |a_k|$?

options.text: The triangle inequality $|x + y| \le |x| + |y|$, applied again and again (by induction on the number of terms).
Because $a_k \le |a_k|$ for each $k$.
options.why: You bounded the sum from above only. A block of $-5$ needs $5 \le \sum |a_k|$ too, which uses $-a_k \le |a_k|$.

options.text: Because the two sides are equal.
options.why: You assumed equality. Signs that differ make the left side smaller: $|1 - 1| = 0 < 2$.

options.text: Because $\sum |a_k|$ converges.
options.why: You used the hypothesis. The inequality holds for every finite block of any series.

hints.text: Start with two terms.
Add one term at a time: that is induction on the triangle inequality.

feedback.correct: Right. The triangle inequality, extended to finitely many terms.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from $|x + y| \le |x| + |y|$.

explain.text: $|x + y| \le |x| + |y|$ handles two terms. Adding one term at a time extends it to any finite block. Cancellation can only make the left side smaller.

screens.title: Absolute convergence implies convergence
screens.prose: Suppose $\sum |a_k|$ converges. Prove that $\sum a_k$ converges, using the Cauchy criterion from l10. Two lines are flawed.
screens.question: Put the proof in order. Move the two flawed lines to Left out.

lines.text: Let $\varepsilon > 0$. The partial sums of $\sum |a_k|$ converge, so they are Cauchy.
So there is $N$ with $\sum_{k=m}^{n} |a_k| < \varepsilon$ for all $n \ge m > N$.
So $(S_n)$ is Cauchy, and Cauchy sequences of reals converge. $\blacksquare$
$|S_n| \le \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} |a_k|$, so $(S_n)$ is bounded and therefore converges.
lines.why: You let bounded mean convergent. The partial sums of $\sum (-1)^n$ are bounded and do not converge.

lines.text: Since $a_k \le |a_k|$, the comparison test gives convergence.
lines.why: You compared terms that may be negative. Comparison needs $0 \le a_k$; with negative terms the sums could fall without bound.

hints.text: Work with blocks of the series, not with a limit.
A block of $\sum a_k$ is $S_n - S_{m-1}$.
Order: Cauchy for the sizes, choose $N$, the triangle inequality on a block, then Cauchy for $(S_n)$.

feedback.correct: Right. The sizes are Cauchy, so the series is.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Bound each block $S_n - S_{m-1}$ by the same block of sizes.

byKey.d1: You used boundedness alone. A bounded sequence can oscillate, as level 2 showed.
byKey.d2: You applied comparison to signed terms. It needs $a_k \ge 0$.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the two flawed lines go to Left out.

explain.text: Every block of $\sum a_k$ is at most the matching block of $\sum |a_k|$ in size. Those blocks are eventually below $\varepsilon$, so $(S_n)$ is Cauchy. Completeness, through l10, supplies the limit.

screens.title: Sort the series
screens.prose: Classify each series: **absolute**, **conditional** or **diverges**. Check $\sum |a_n|$ first, then the alternating series test.
screens.question: Type absolute, conditional or diverges in each row.

hints.text: For each row, ask first whether $\sum |a_n|$ converges.
$\sum \tfrac{1}{\sqrt n}$ diverges, since $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt n} \ge \tfrac1n$; $\sum \tfrac{n}{2^n}$ converges by the ratio test.
$(-1)^n$ does not tend to 0, so that series diverges.

feedback.correct: Right. Conditional, absolute, diverges, conditional, absolute.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Test absolute values first, then the alternating series test, then the term test.

byKey.r2c1: $\sum (-1)^n$ alternates, but its terms have size 1, not tending to 0. The term test says it diverges.
byKey.r3c1: $\sum \tfrac{1}{\sqrt n}$ diverges, yet $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt n}$ decreases to 0. So the series converges, conditionally.
byKey.r1c1: $\sum \tfrac1{n^2}$ converges, so this one converges absolutely.
byKey.r0c1: $\sum \tfrac1n$ diverges, but the alternating series test applies: conditional.

explain.text: Absolute when the sizes sum: $\tfrac1{n^2}$ and $\tfrac{n}{2^n}$. Conditional when the sizes diverge but decrease to 0: $\tfrac1n$ and $\tfrac1{\sqrt n}$. The edge case $\sum (-1)^n$ alternates, yet its terms do not tend to 0, so it diverges.

screens.title: Alternating, shrinking, diverging
screens.prose: Take sizes $1, 1, \tfrac12, \tfrac14, \tfrac13, \tfrac19, \tfrac14, \tfrac1{16}, \dots$: $\tfrac1k$ in the odd places, $\tfrac1{k^2}$ in the even ones. They tend to 0. Alternate the signs: $1 - 1 + \tfrac12 - \tfrac14 + \tfrac13 - \tfrac19 + \cdots$ The dots are its partial sums.
screens.question: Does the series converge?

options.text: No: $S_{2k} = \sum_{j=1}^{k} \left(\tfrac1j - \tfrac1{j^2}\right)$, and $\sum \tfrac1j$ diverges while $\sum \tfrac1{j^2}$ converges, so $S_{2k} \to \infty$.
Yes, by the alternating series test.
options.why: You skipped a hypothesis. The sizes are not decreasing: $\tfrac14$ is followed by $\tfrac13$.

options.text: Yes: the signs alternate and the terms tend to 0.
options.why: You kept two hypotheses and dropped the third. Without decreasing sizes the swings up can outweigh the swings down.

options.text: No, because the terms do not tend to 0.
options.why: You blamed the terms. They do tend to 0; the failure is that they do not decrease.

hints.text: Group the terms in pairs: one up, one down.
Pair $k$ is $\tfrac1k - \tfrac1{k^2}$.
$\sum \tfrac1k$ diverges and $\sum \tfrac1{k^2}$ converges, so their difference diverges.

feedback.correct: Right. Drop decreasing, and the test fails.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the terms in pairs and compare with the harmonic series.

byKey.ast: You used the alternating series test without its hypothesis. Its proof needs $a_{2n+1} - a_{2n+2} \ge 0$, and here $\tfrac14 < \tfrac13$.

explain.text: Pair $k$ adds $\tfrac1k - \tfrac1{k^2} \ge 0$, and these pairs sum like the harmonic series. So $S_{2k} \to \infty$; here $S_{40} \approx 2.0016$ and still climbing. Each hypothesis of the test, decreasing included, is needed.

screens.title: The bound against the truth
screens.prose: Write `alt_partial(n)`, `terms_needed(eps)`, the smallest $n$ with $\tfrac{1}{n+1} < \varepsilon$ (what the bound guarantees), and `actual_needed(eps)`, the smallest $n$ with $|\ln 2 - S_n| < \varepsilon$. The true error shrinks as $n$ grows.
screens.question: Complete the three functions.

widget.starter:
from fractions import Fraction
import math

def alt_partial(n):
    """S_n of 1 - 1/2 + 1/3 - ... (n terms), as a float."""
    ...

def terms_needed(eps):
    """Smallest n with 1/(n+1) < eps. eps is a Fraction."""
    ...

def actual_needed(eps):
    """Smallest n with |ln 2 - S_n| < eps (the true error)."""
    ...
widget.how: Check runs 12 hidden tests. alt_partial is compared with math.isclose within absolute 1e-9. terms_needed takes exact Fractions, including the boundary 1/1000. actual_needed takes floats from 0.1 to 0.0005 and is compared exactly.

hints.text: `alt_partial` adds `(-1) ** (k + 1) / k`.
For `terms_needed`, loop while `Fraction(1, n + 1) >= eps`; equality is not yet enough.
For `actual_needed`, add terms one at a time and stop when `abs(math.log(2) - s) < eps`.

feedback.correct: Right. The bound asks for 1000 terms; 500 already suffice.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the bound's comparison strict and exact, and stop `actual_needed` at the first small error.

explain.text: The bound $\tfrac{1}{n+1} < 0.001$ needs $n = 1000$, but the true error falls below 0.001 at $n = 500$, where it is about 0.000999. The true error is close to $\tfrac{1}{2n}$, half the bound. The bound is honest and twice as cautious as needed.

screens.title: Net small, gross unbounded
screens.prose: Trade $n$ of a strategy has size £$\tfrac{1000}{n}$ and gains or loses it, alternately: $+\text{£}1{,}000$, $-\text{£}500$, $+\text{£}333$, and so on. The net P&L tends to $1000 \ln 2 \approx \text{£}693$. The amount traded is the sum of the sizes.
screens.question: What is the amount traded after 1,000 trades? Give the nearest pound.

hints.text: The amount traded is $1000\left(1 + \tfrac12 + \cdots + \tfrac1{1000}\right) = 1000 H_{1000}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the sizes, not the signed P&L.

byKey.net: You gave the net P&L. The amount traded adds every size, gains and losses alike.
byKey.lnn: You used $1000 \ln 1000$ and dropped Euler's constant. $H_n \approx \ln n + 0.5772$.

explain.text: The net converges conditionally, to £693, while the amount traded is $1000 H_n$, which diverges. A 1% cost on volume is £74.85 after 1,000 trades and about £143.93 after a million. A conditionally convergent net hides an unbounded gross.

ideas: Alternating series test: if $a_n$ decreases to 0, the even sums rise, the odd sums fall, and both meet; $|S - S_n| \le a_{n+1}$.
Absolute convergence ($\sum |a_n|$ converges) implies convergence: blocks obey $\left|\sum_{k=m}^n a_k\right| \le \sum_{k=m}^n |a_k|$, so $(S_n)$ is Cauchy.
Conditional convergence: $\sum \tfrac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n}$ converges to $\ln 2$ while $\sum \tfrac1n$ diverges.
summary.trap: Alternating signs and terms tending to 0 are not enough. The sizes must also decrease, or the sums can climb for ever.

quiz.prose: A colleague says: $\sum \tfrac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n}$ converges, so it converges absolutely.
quiz.question: Is the colleague right?

options.text: No: absolute convergence needs $\sum \tfrac1n$ to converge, and it diverges. The convergence is conditional.
Yes: a convergent series converges absolutely.
options.why: You reversed the theorem. Absolute implies convergent; this series shows the converse fails.

options.text: Yes: the alternating series test proves absolute convergence.
options.why: You credited the test with too much. It proves convergence only, and here $\sum |a_n|$ diverges.

options.text: No: the series diverges.
options.why: You dropped the signs. With them the series converges, to $\ln 2$.

explain.text: Absolute convergence asks for $\sum \left|\tfrac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n}\right| = \sum \tfrac1n$, which diverges. The series itself converges by the alternating series test. So it converges conditionally.

quiz.prose: $\sum \tfrac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n^2}$ has decreasing sizes tending to 0. Its sum is $\tfrac{\pi^2}{12}$.
quiz.question: What bound does the alternating series test give for $\left|\tfrac{\pi^2}{12} - S_5\right|$?

feedback.correct: Right. $\tfrac1{36}$; the true error is about 0.0161.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The bound is $a_6$.

byKey.same: You used $a_5 = \tfrac1{25}$, the last term added. The bound is the next size, $a_6 = \tfrac1{36}$.

explain.text: $|S - S_5| \le a_6 = \tfrac{1}{36} \approx 0.0278$. In fact $S_5 \approx 0.838611$ and $\tfrac{\pi^2}{12} \approx 0.822467$, an error of 0.016144. The bound holds with room to spare.

quiz.question: Does the alternating series test apply?

options.text: No: the sizes are all 1, so they do not tend to 0. The series diverges by the term test.
Yes: the signs alternate, so it converges.
options.why: You checked only the signs. The test also needs sizes decreasing to 0.

options.text: Yes, and the sum is 0.
options.why: You bracketed in pairs. That keeps the even partial sums, all 0; the odd ones are $-1$.

options.text: Yes, and the sum is $-\tfrac12$.
options.why: You averaged the partial sums. They swing between $-1$ and 0 with no limit.

feedback.correct: Right. Alternating signs alone are not enough.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check every hypothesis of the test.

explain.text: The sizes are constant at 1, so they neither decrease strictly nor tend to 0. The partial sums run $-1, 0, -1, 0, \dots$ The term test settles it: the series diverges.

quiz.question: What is the smallest $n$ for which the bound guarantees an error below 0.001?

byKey.sqrt: You found $n + 1 = 32$. The question asks for $n$, which is 31.
byKey.lin: You solved $\tfrac{1}{n+1} < 0.001$. The sizes here are $\tfrac{1}{(n+1)^2}$.

explain.text: $\tfrac{1}{(n+1)^2} < 0.001$ means $(n+1)^2 > 1000$. Since $31^2 = 961$ and $32^2 = 1024$, we need $n + 1 = 32$. Absolutely convergent series with fast-shrinking sizes need far fewer terms.
